content: Althaea officinalis, commonly known as marshmallow, marsh mallow, or common marshmallow, is a plant species native to Africa. It is utilized both as a medicinal plant and as an ornamental plant. The stems of the plant are upright, reaching heights of 3 to 4 feet. They die back in autumn and are either simple or produce only a few lateral branches. The leaves are short-stalked, roundish, and ovate-cordate in shape, measuring 2 to 3 inches in length and about 1.25 inches in width. They may be entire or divided into three to five lobes, with irregularly toothed margins. The leaves are thick and covered on both sides with a dense layer of stellate hairs, giving them a soft, velvety texture. The flowers resemble those of the common mallow but are smaller and pale in color. They are either axillary or arranged in panicles, with the latter being more common. The stamens are fused into a tube, and the anthers are kidney-shaped and single-celled. The flowers bloom in August and September, followed by flat, round fruits commonly referred to as cheeses. While the common mallow is often called marsh mallow by rural populations, the true marshmallow is distinguished by its numerous divisions in the outer calyx (six to nine clefts), the hoary down that densely covers its stems and foliage, and the numerous panicles of pale blush-colored flowers. The roots of Althaea officinalis are perennial, thick, long, and tapering. They are tough, pliant, and whitish-yellow on the outside, with a white, fibrous interior. The entire plant, particularly the root, contains a mild mucilage that is significantly more emollient than that of the common mallow. The generic name Althaea is derived from the Greek word altho, meaning to cure, reflecting its healing properties. The family name Malvaceae comes from the Greek word malake, meaning soft, referring to the plant's mucilaginous and soothing qualities. Historically, many mallow species have been used as food. The Romans considered marshmallow an edible vegetable, and it was regarded as a delicacy. The Chinese also incorporate certain types of mallow into their cuisine, and in 1592, Prosper Alpinus noted that a mallow-like plant was consumed by Egyptians. In Syria, particularly among poorer populations such as the Fellahs, Greeks, and Armenians, marshmallow is a common food source during times of scarcity. The roots, when boiled and fried with onions and butter, are said to make a palatable dish. In times of crop failure, the plant, which grows abundantly in the region, is widely collected for sustenance. The leaves, flowers, and roots of Althaea officinalis possess medicinal properties. The leaves, harvested in summer as the plant begins to flower, have demulcent, expectorant, diuretic, and emollient properties. They are commonly used to treat ailments of the lungs and urinary systems, including urethritis and kidney stones. The roots, harvested in late autumn, also have demulcent, diuretic, emollient, and vulnerary properties. They are known to increase breast milk production, soothe the bronchial tubes, and are used to treat constipation and irritable bowel syndrome. Externally, the roots are applied to varicose veins, ulcers, abscesses, and boils. Additionally, root extracts are sometimes used as flavoring in Middle Eastern snacks such as halva. The historical and folkloric use of marshmallow is extensive. The plant was used as early as 200 BC under its Greek name Althea, meaning to heal. The family name Malvaceae reflects the plant's soft, mucilaginous nature. Theophrastus (circa 372–286 BC) reported its use in sweet wine for treating coughs. Hippocrates described its value in wound treatment, while Dioscorides recommended a vinegar infusion for toothaches and a preparation of the seeds to soothe insect stings. The Roman poet Horace noted its laxative properties. During the Renaissance, herbalists used marshmallow for sore throats, stomach problems, gonorrhea, leukorrhea, and as a gargle for oral infections. In medieval times, marshmallow was associated with trials of innocence. It was believed that an ointment made from the plant could protect the accused from burns when holding a red-hot iron bar. Accounts from the Middle Ages also suggest that anointing the palms with marshmallow ointment could prevent burns, regardless of guilt or innocence. Pliny the Elder claimed that consuming a spoonful of mallow would protect one from all diseases for the day. The plant was also known as the Mortification Plant for its use in treating wounds. Marshmallow ointments were believed to ward off evil and cast out demons. The plant's edible properties are reflected in its name, as marshmallow creme and candies were originally derived from the root of the plant. Mallows are even mentioned in the Bible, in the Book of Job, as a food source during times of famine.
